meta.title: Chevir - real-time translation between the speech- and hearing-impaired and the hearing
meta.description: Chevir - real-time two-way translation between Azerbaijani Sign Language and spoken Azerbaijani. We are looking for pilot partners.
meta.ogImageAlt: Chevir logo with the tagline "Sign language, made audible."
statement.line1: Chevir is an AI-based software solution that translates sign language into text, and text into sign language.
statement.line2: Given that Azerbaijan has 13,000 speech- and hearing-impaired people,
statement.line3: it was created to make communication in Azerbaijani Sign Language easier for them.
pipeline.heading: How it works
pipeline.lead: Communication with sign language users becomes easier in both directions - signs are translated into text, and text into sign language.
pipeline.step.0.title: Vision and tracking
pipeline.step.0.desc: The camera tracks hand, finger and facial movements in real time and records the sequence of AzSL (Azerbaijani Sign Language) signs.
pipeline.step.0.videoDesc: Video: the camera tracks hand and finger movements with keypoints.
pipeline.step.1.title: Recognition
pipeline.step.1.desc: The model recognizes the signs; an attention map shows which points of the hand shape it relied on.
pipeline.step.1.videoDesc: Video: the model's attention map shows, with a colored overlay, which points of the hand shape it relied on.
pipeline.step.2.title: Translation and voice
pipeline.step.2.desc: Recognized signs are converted into spoken Azerbaijani and delivered by voice or as text.
pipeline.step.3.title: Reply in sign language
pipeline.step.3.desc: The hearing person's reply is converted into AzSL and shown in sign language by an avatar. This feature is at the prototype stage.
pipeline.step.3.videoDesc: Video: the avatar turns text into sign language and signs it.
loop.heading: Chevir closes the loop in both directions
loop.lead: A speech- or hearing-impaired citizen's signing is converted into text and speech, and the hearing person's reply returns as sign language. Neither side has to wait.
loop.side.signed.title: Hearing-impaired person
loop.side.signed.desc: Signs in sign language, looking at the camera.
loop.side.spoken.title: Social service agent
loop.side.spoken.desc: Hears in spoken language and responds.
problem.stat.desc: Estimated number of speech- and hearing-impaired people in Azerbaijan.
problem.heading: Writing is not a solution, it is a barrier.
problem.paragraph1: A person born with hearing loss never hears Azerbaijani. They learn it as a second language. Filling in a form at a clinic or reading a bank contract is, for them, like filling in a document in a foreign language.
problem.paragraph2: Existing accessibility tools work in only one direction: from the hearing person to the speech- or hearing-impaired person. Subtitles exist. The opposite direction - what is said in sign language reaching the hearing person - is completely empty.
difference.heading: What sets us apart
difference.item.0.title: One skeleton, two directions
difference.item.0.desc: Recognition and generation are not separate systems. Both draw on the same skeleton representation - the points extracted from the camera are used both to read a sign and to animate the avatar. This ensures the two directions match at the architecture level.
difference.item.1.title: Facial expression is not an afterthought
difference.item.1.desc: In sign language, negation, questions and conditions are conveyed through facial and head movements. The field's leading commercial player calls fluent generation of these elements an unsolved problem. For us, this is not a later improvement - it is a starting requirement of the architecture.
difference.item.2.title: Verified with the community
difference.item.2.desc: Model outputs are checked not by laboratory metrics, but by the level of understanding of people whose native language is sign language. This prevents results that look successful in theory but are not understood in practice.
values.slogan: The slogan of the speech- and hearing-impaired community.
values.principle: A speech- or hearing-impaired user will never have to pay to read or create content in their native language. Accessibility cannot sit behind a paywall.
usecases.heading: Where it works
usecases.item.0.title: Government services and banks
usecases.item.0.desc: Direct translation at application desks, service counters and call centers.
usecases.item.1.title: Healthcare
usecases.item.1.desc: Communication between doctor and patient in urgent and scheduled appointments.
usecases.item.2.title: Education
usecases.item.2.desc: Real-time translation in the classroom and at parent-teacher meetings.
usecases.item.3.title: Digital platforms
usecases.item.3.desc: A translation layer that integrates into apps and websites via API.
results.heading: Current results
results.lead: The following are real outputs of models trained on AzSLD (Azerbaijani Sign Language Dataset).
results.accuracy.desc: AzSLD - accuracy of our recognition model trained on 30,000 annotated videos.
results.accuracy.caveat: Figures above 95% are usually announced in this field. But that figure is obtained when videos of the same people appear in both training and testing. When the model has to recognize a new person it has never seen, accuracy drops to 62%. We do not show the first figure at all.
results.card.0.title: Prediction
results.card.0.desc: The original footage and the model's prediction are compared side by side.
results.card.1.title: Recognition output
results.card.1.desc: The recognized sign is converted into text and speech output.

impact.line1: In Azerbaijan, how speech- and hearing-impaired people communicate depends either on interpreters or on family members.
impact.line2: Chevir changes this and aims to help people whose native language is sign language regain their place in society.
roadmap.heading: Roadmap
roadmap.item.0.title: Translation API for web platforms
roadmap.item.0.desc: A translation service that banks, government and healthcare systems can integrate directly.
roadmap.item.1.title: Standalone mobile app
roadmap.item.1.desc: An app that hearing users and speech- or hearing-impaired users can use directly from their own phones.
roadmap.item.2.title: Platform and dataset expansion
roadmap.item.2.desc: Dataset growth for a wider sign vocabulary and new areas of use.

trust.lead: Chevir is not starting from scratch - behind it are published research, an open dataset and real collaboration with the community.

team.heading: Team
team.member.0.name: Sitara Aghayeva
team.member.0.bio: Seven years of experience in data science and machine learning, and four years in risk management. Holds a master's degree from IU International University of Applied Sciences and an international Risk and Artificial Intelligence certification. Leads Chevir's execution and pilot partnerships.
team.member.1.name: Lala Ibadullayeva
team.member.1.bio: PhD candidate in computational structural biology at the ANAS Institute of Molecular Biology; builds artificial intelligence solutions at Baku State University. Research experience at Cambridge MRC LMB. Leads the deep learning research behind Chevir's motion recognition and sign translation models.
team.member.2.name: Nigar Alishzade
team.member.2.bio: PhD candidate, computer science lecturer at Karabakh University and executive member of the "Karlara Dəstək" Public Union. Author of the AzSLD dataset and several papers on sign language recognition. Leads Chevir's technology development and community relations.
